label: AQ 0029
title: The filter that only learned from wins

questions.q: Isn't filtering by reward just RL anyway?
questions.a: Half true. DeepSeekMath writes both as the same gradient: the filter weights each answer 1 if correct and 0 if wrong, while GRPO subtracts the group's average score (a baseline), so failures get pushed down and solved tasks stop counting. So the filter is policy gradient with the crudest weights and no baseline.

questions.q: How would you get signal on tasks the model never passes?
questions.a: Neither method can alone: a task that always fails gives zero weight. STaR showed the model the correct answer and had it write the reasoning (“rationalization”). Other options: easier stepping-stone tasks, more attempts on hard ones, or distillation (training on a stronger model's answers), which Yue et al. say “can introduce new reasoning patterns”.

teach.title: How it works: when the filter is enough, and where it stalls

questions.q: How many rounds of the loop would you run?
questions.a: Until a held-out set stops improving, which may be soon. ReST-EM found that more than a couple of rounds gave diminishing gains, and on the APPS coding benchmark the second round got worse, which the authors suspect was overfitting to the small set of training problems.

teach.title: How it works: when the filter is enough, and where it stalls

questions.q: In DeepSeekMath's unified view, how do rejection-sampling fine-tuning and GRPO weight each sampled answer?
questions.a: Rejection-sampling fine-tuning gives weight 1 to correct answers and 0 to wrong ones. GRPO uses the answer's reward minus the group's mean, divided by the group's spread, so wrong answers get pushed down and rare successes count more.

teach.title: How it works: when the filter is enough, and where it stalls

questions.q: Why does plain rejection sampling over-weight easy problems, and how did ReST-EM guard against it?
questions.a: An easy problem yields many passing samples, a hard one few, so easy problems fill the training set. ReST-EM capped the kept solutions at 10 per problem.

teach.title: How it works: when the filter is enough, and where it stalls

questions.q: What did Yue et al. (NeurIPS 2025) find when comparing RL-trained models with their base models?
questions.a: RL-trained models did better with one attempt, but base models scored higher when allowed many attempts, so the authors conclude the reasoning abilities are “bounded by the base model”.
